content: One recurring issue in interpreting studies on vitamin A supplementation in children is the GRADE criteria of indirectness. Many studies included both well-nourished and malnourished children, which limited the ability to draw direct conclusions about the efficacy of vitamin A in treating severe acute malnutrition (SAM). As a result, conclusions could only be made through subgroup analyses. Two review studies that included both well-nourished and malnourished children demonstrated reductions in mortality in large-scale, community-based trials. These effects were more frequently observed in Asia and were particularly notable for diarrhea-related mortality. One of these reviews also included hospital-based trials, which found that vitamin A supplementation reduced the severity of measles and diarrheal diseases but increased the risk of acute lower respiratory infections (ALRI). Evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) reviewed suggests several conclusions regarding vitamin A and SAM. First, low-dose vitamin A supplementation (5,000 IU daily) until hospital discharge was more effective in reducing mortality, severe diarrhea incidence, and respiratory infection incidence and duration in children with edema compared to a single high-dose vitamin A supplementation (200,000 IU for children >12 months; 100,000 IU for children ≤12 months) given on the first day of hospital admission. Second, high-dose vitamin A supplementation may be beneficial for treating severely malnourished children with severe diarrhea or shigellosis. However, there is no evidence supporting the efficacy or safety of vitamin A supplementation in severely malnourished children presenting with non-measles pneumonia or other ALRI. Some trials showed positive outcomes, while others reported adverse events or no significant findings associated with vitamin A supplementation. High-dose vitamin A supplementation was effective in treating measles-specific respiratory illness in severely malnourished children. However, no evidence was identified that directly examined the outcomes related to the timing of high-dose vitamin A supplementation in children with SAM. Finally, the review found some evidence of positive growth outcomes associated with vitamin A supplementation after hospital discharge in severely malnourished children. In two trials, vitamin A supplementation at discharge was associated with weight gain during the follow-up period. However, this evidence is relatively dated and limited, necessitating further research. Future studies should explore the use of ready-to-use therapeutic foods (RUTF), community-based management of acute malnutrition (CMAM), and vitamin A supplementation to improve outcomes in this population. Further research is needed to replicate findings on the efficacy of low-dose vitamin A supplementation in treating severely malnourished children with edema, severe diarrhea, or shigellosis. Additionally, more studies are required to evaluate the effectiveness of various strategies to improve vitamin A nutrition (e.g., supplementation, RUTF, dietary improvements) after hospital discharge in children treated for SAM.
